comparison: Both evaluate microbiome characterization data (C22-C31) positively. OpenEval finds the 16S rRNA and ITS2 sequencing data well-supported with appropriate statistical tests. Peer review describes the comprehensive gene expression and microbiome analysis as 'compelling and goes beyond the current state of the art,' with the reviewer acknowledging it as 'somewhat useful and important for the TB field.'

Both evaluate trans-kingdom network analysis (C32-C40) positively. OpenEval finds the network analysis data well-supported with clear quantitative differences and appropriate statistical significance. Peer review implicitly accepts these findings as part of the 'compelling' data that 'goes beyond the current state of the art,' with no specific critique of the network analysis.

Both evaluate RNA-seq analysis (C59-C73) positively. OpenEval finds the comprehensive RNA-seq analysis well-supported with appropriate statistical thresholds and RT-qPCR validation. Peer review specifically praises the 'comprehensive analysis of gene expression profiles' as 'compelling and goes beyond the current state of the art,' with the reviewer acknowledging it provides useful 'overview of gene pathways and critical genes.'

Both evaluate in vitro Nos2 experiments (C74-C80) but with different assessments. OpenEval finds the data supported though notes need for protein-level validation and additional mechanistic experiments. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, with editor stating mechanistic insights are 'currently incomplete' and reviewer criticizing that A549 cell line experiments 'may not be enough' since A549 is not the primary Mtb infection target.

Both evaluate clindamycin model data (C15-C21) but with different assessments. OpenEval finds the experimental data well-supported with appropriate controls and statistical significance. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, with editor noting data is 'compelling' but reviewer criticizing use of MS instead of 'wide-type Mtb strain (e.g. H37Rv)' and questioning clinical significance of MS-infected mouse models.

Both evaluate overall conclusions and proposed mechanisms (C114-C116) but with different assessments. OpenEval finds conclusions well-supported by comprehensive experimental evidence while acknowledging limitations. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, with editor noting mechanistic insights and Mtb experiments are 'currently incomplete' and reviewer criticizing reliance on MS models lacking clinical significance and failure to examine lung pathology.

Both evaluate gut-lung axis background claims (C5-C13 for OpenEval, C1-C13 for peer review). OpenEval finds these literature-based claims appropriately cited and supported. Peer review also accepts these contextual background statements without challenge, as they are standard literature-based information.

Both evaluate FMT experiments (C41-C52 for OpenEval, C41-C58 for peer review). OpenEval finds the FMT model establishment well-supported with successful recapitulation of donor dysbiosis. Peer review accepts the FMT data as part of 'compelling' evidence showing 'the effect of gut dysbiosis on the colonization of mycobacteria in the lung,' with no specific critique of FMT methodology.

Both evaluate discussion/literature contextualization (C81-C101 for OpenEval, C81-C112 for peer review). OpenEval finds the literature citations appropriate and notes the discussion appropriately acknowledges contradictions in NO/Nos2 literature. Peer review accepts these literature-based discussion points without specific challenge, though broader concerns about clinical significance and model choice affect overall interpretation.

Both evaluate epidemiological background claims (C1-C4 for OpenEval, C1-C13 for peer review). OpenEval finds these WHO and literature-based epidemiological facts appropriately referenced. Peer review accepts these standard background claims without challenge.

Both address FMT causality experiments. OpenEval evaluates C53-C58 specifically on MS colonization and gut permeability mechanisms, finding them well-supported. Peer review evaluates broader FMT claims (C41-C58) and accepts the causal link between gut dysbiosis and lung susceptibility as 'compelling,' though with partial overlap in claim coverage.

Both evaluate discussion of ROS and Defb1 mechanisms (C103-C112). OpenEval finds the literature citations appropriate and notes the Defb1-MS correlation is a reasonable inference from experimental data. Peer review accepts these literature-based discussion points without specific challenge.

OpenEval evaluates C102 (NO dose-dependent speculation) as UNCERTAIN, noting it is explicitly speculative and not directly tested. Peer review R8 covers C81-C112 including C102, accepting literature-based discussion points generally but with broader concerns about clinical significance that may relate to speculative claims.
